title: Stronger Seed Banks, Increased Fertilizer Production Vital to Boost Africa’s Agricultural Productivity
desc:
Addis Ababa, August 17, 2026 (ENA) —The African Union has called for stronger seed banks to conserve indigenous crop varieties and increased investment in domestic fertilizer production to boost agricultural productivity across the continent.
Moses Vilakati, African Union Commissioner for Agriculture, Rural Development, Blue Economy and Sustainable Environment, said Africa has 60 percent of the world’s uncultivated arable land, yet spends more than 100 billion USD annually on food imports.
A two-day consultation on agricultural transformation among member states of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD) and the implementation of the Kampala Declaration, which will run from 2026 to 2035, began in Addis Ababa today.
The consultation is reviewing the two-year implementation report of the fifth Comprehensive Africa Agriculture Development Programme (CAADP) and assessing progress at the regional level within IGAD.
Speaking at the forum, Commissioner Vilakati said the two-year review period under the Malabo Declaration had come to an end, stressing that the next phase should focus on effective implementation and delivering tangible results.
He said the Kampala Agenda has set targets for Africa to increase agricultural production by 45 percent by 2035, triple intra-African trade, reduce post-harvest losses by 50 percent and mobilize 100 billion USD in investment.
Vilakati emphasized the need to improve soil health, strengthen seed banks that conserve indigenous crop varieties and develop domestic fertilizer production by utilizing Africa’s phosphate and potash resources.
He said achieving the targets would require stronger investment in agricultural inputs, technologies and systems that can increase productivity and strengthen the continent’s food security.
The Commissioner also stressed that the success of the Kampala Agenda should ultimately be measured by the improvements it brings to the lives and livelihoods of people across the continent.
Meanwhile, Sylvia Henga, who delivered remarks on behalf of the Director of IGAD’s Agriculture and Environment Division, said conflict, carbon emissions, climate change and displacement are adversely affecting the agricultural sector in the region.
She noted that irrigation use in the region remains below 20 percent and said IGAD is implementing soil information systems and early warning mechanisms to strengthen agricultural resilience.
Zena Habtewold, Advisor to the Minister of Agriculture and Ethiopia’s representative for the programme, said Ethiopia is working with various stakeholders to translate the Kampala Agenda into locally driven approaches.
He added that Ethiopia is implementing a number of programmes aimed at contributing significantly to the agricultural sector, including the “Lemat Tirufat” initiative.

title: Anomalous quantum oscillations reveal new physics in a topological insulator
desc: A study has been published in Nature Communications that identifies an unusual regime of quantum oscillations in a three-dimensional topological insulator. The results show that, when subjected to temperatures near absolute zero and extreme magnetic fields, electrons in the material zirconium pentatelluride (ZrTe₅) exhibit behavior that deviates from the pattern predicted by conventional theory.

title: Intervention program reduces children's anxiety and improves functional ability
desc: A new follow-up study examined the efficacy of the Master Your Worries program developed by the Research Center for Child Psychiatry at the University of Turku in Finland. It involved 465 Finnish children ages 10–13 who showed symptoms of anxiety. The children were screened during annual school health checkups. No similar study using a population-based screening program to identify anxiety in children and provide remote care has been published previously.
